items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: tanstack router vs react router, my two cents
items.summary: Every React app I have ever shipped used React Router. It was never a decision. It was just what you did, like npm install and a src folder and arguing about semicolons in code review. Then TanStack Router started showing up everywhere I looked. I spent a weekend reading both sets of docs side by side, and here is the honest version, no fanboy stuff either way. React Router v7 landed in late 2024 and merged with Remix, so it is a different animal than the v6 most of us learned. Everything lives in one package now, just react-router, and there are three modes: declarative (the classic Routes and Route components), data (createBrowserRouter with loaders and actions), and framework (file-based routes with SSR, basically the old Remix life). It is the safe default. Ten years of Stack Overflow answers exist for every problem you will hit. Type safety, end to end. That is the pitch, and it is a good one. You define a route tree, and TypeScript knows your params and your search params everywhere. Navigate to a route with the wrong params and you get a red squiggle in your editor instead of a blank page at runtime. It is at version 1.170 as I write this, and it is very actively maintained.

items.title: How We Built a 3-Layer JS + WebAssembly Crackme to Stress-Test Code Defense Against AI Decompilers
items.summary: Traditional JavaScript and WebAssembly obfuscators rely on lexical cosmetic tricks: renaming variables to _0x4a2b, base64-encoding string arrays, and wrapping functions in simple switch statements. While those techniques slow down casual inspection in browser DevTools, modern static semantic graph extractors (morluto/rea), native decompilers (NSA Ghidra, WABT wasm-decompile), and LLM-driven reverse-engineering agents slice through them in seconds. An LLM does not care what a variable is named; it reads the data-flow graph and reconstructs clean source code. To solve this at the compiler level, we built Syferit (github.com/soltrix-studios/syferit), an open-core (v1.0.2) multi-target code defense engine for JavaScript/TypeScript, WebAssembly, Python, and C/C++ (LLVM). Instead of asking developers to take our word for it, we shipped a live 60 FPS browser game and 3-layer reverse-engineering crackme: SYFER-DEFENDER: The Three-Layer Override. items.title: React Signup Flows Need a Testable Email Boundary
items.summary: Signup email is usually treated like a small feature: submit a form, send a message, then show a success state. In a real React product, it becomes a boundary between browser state, an API, a mail provider, and a test inbox. When those concerns leak into each other, the UI gets hard to reason about and the tests become slow or flaky. I have found it more useful to treat email delivery as a replaceable product dependency. The React screen should know that a verification request was accepted. It should not know if the message went through a provider API, a local fake, or a disposable email account used by an end-to-end test. That separation makes a signup flow easier to ship, and it gives the team a cleaner place to inspect failures. The same idea works when a team searches for “temp mail so” while setting up a test workflow: the search phrase may vary, but the application still needs a stable contract. items.title: Test the bad import before the overwrite button
items.summary: A broken project file should not get to ask whether it can replace your work. In my downloadable browser chart editor, opening a saved project can replace the chart someone is editing. I added a confirmation for unsaved changes, then tested the order of operations. The important case was not clicking OK. It was uploading an invalid file while edits were waiting. My import path follows this order: Read and parse the candidate file. Validate its project format and values without changing the current editor. If the current editor has unsaved changes, ask whether to replace them. Apply the validated project only after acceptance. Record the imported state as the new clean baseline. If validation fails, the existing chart stays in place. There is no overwrite question because there is no usable replacement to approve. That distinction matters for a chart editor. A file can be valid JSON but contain unusable chart data. Parsing is not the same as validating the project. items.summary: Originally published at hamzaahmadaslam.com. How this article was made: drafted with AI assistance from a researched brief, then checked against primary documentation before publishing. To audit WordPress third party scripts, start by listing every external dependency and the business owner who still needs it, then measure its network and main-thread cost. Change one dependency at a time, compare the same page and user flow, and retest consent, forms, analytics, and checkout before you remove or delay anything. Third-party JavaScript is code you did not author and that is served by another provider. It can add network requests, CPU work, rendering delays, and dependencies on servers you do not control. Google’s third-party JavaScript performance guide also recommends routine audits and removing redundant providers. Do not stop at the domain name. Record who added the dependency, who owns its business purpose, and what would fail if it disappeared. A marketing pixel with no current campaign owner deserves a different decision from a payment script that checkout needs. Use this worksheet as the working record. items.title: Why the download button waits for your tap
items.summary: Paste a TikTok link into ramrom.io, and nothing happens. No spinner, no automatic resolve, no file dropping into your downloads folder. The page just waits. That is deliberate, and it is one of the easiest decisions I made while building the site. The temptation to auto-download is real. Every downloader I tested before building mine did something on paste. It felt slick in a demo: paste, and the video is already on its way. So when I wired up the paste event on the link box, my first version did the obvious thing. Paste a link, and the page fired the resolve call straight away, then started the download the moment a file URL came back. It worked. It also felt wrong the first time I used it for real. The first problem is that a paste is not a decision. People paste a link to check it, to compare it, to see whether the site even supports that platform. Sometimes they paste the wrong link entirely — a share URL copied in a hurry, or a link to a private video. If the site has already fired a resolve call, that mistake has cost an API call. items.title: NSApp.activate raised every window of my Mac app, so scroll capture scrolled the wrong one
items.summary: I make Scry, a screenshot app for the Mac. One of its tools is scroll capture: you draw a box around part of a page, and Scry scrolls that page and stitches one long image. For a while it had a bug that looked random. You drew the box over a web page, and Scry scrolled its own Library window instead. Sometimes it scrolled the Settings window. Never the page you asked for. The cause was one line I had added on purpose. The capture overlay is a borderless, full-screen, transparent window. To take key and receive keystrokes, the app has to be active, so the overlay called: NSApp.activate(ignoringOtherApps: true) That does make the overlay key. It also orders every ordinary window of the app above every other app. With a transparent overlay covering the whole screen, nobody sees it happen. You only see the result afterwards: the Library is now the top window under your box, and that is what gets scrolled. items.title: Getting the Raw Request Body for Webhook Verification in 8 Frameworks
items.summary: Most signature mismatches come from the framework parsing the JSON before you verify it. We show how to read the raw request body and verify a webhook in Express, Next.js, Hono, FastAPI, Django, Rails, Laravel and Go. A webhook signature is computed over the bytes the sender put on the wire. Parse the JSON and serialize it again and you change whitespace, key order or how numbers and Unicode are written, and the signature no longer matches. The fix is always the same: read the body of the webhook route before any JSON parser runs. This post shows how in eight frameworks, with minimal verification code for each. The examples use the Standard Webhooks format that Webhook Admin sends (webhook-id, webhook-timestamp, webhook-signature). Node examples verify with the webhookadmin npm package; Python, Ruby and Go use the official Standard Webhooks libraries; PHP uses built-in functions. Reading the raw body works the same way for Stripe, GitHub or anyone else. Framework behavior was checked against official docs on 2026-09-27. items.title: Daily Coding Wins
items.summary: I count a bug fixed when the exact steps that broke it stop breaking it. The edit is the middle of the job, not the end of it. I squashed a bug in React last week, and the satisfying part was not the change. It was running the same steps that broke it and watching them pass. Debugging is puzzles, one piece at a time. That is the line I wrote to myself when I started the day, and it held up. Each piece is a fact I can check: what the state was before the break, what changed between the working run and the broken one, what the render did with the value it was given. A piece I cannot check is not a piece. It is a guess wearing a puzzle shape. The method is the same one I use on the backend. Reproduce it first, before touching anything. Shrink it until only one thing can be wrong. Change that one thing. Then run the exact steps again. If the steps still break, the fix was a guess, and I say so and keep going. The same discipline sits behind the SES piece I published in October: an accepted call is not a delivered message, and a green run is not a fixed bug. The check is the win, not the edit. I have rebuilt this form more times than I would like to admit. This post is the version I now start from, using Laravel, Inertia and React: one useForm holding the header and the lines, stable row keys, validation errors that land on the right row, live totals that never touch floats, and a server that recalculates everything anyway. items.title: Our contact form runs four checks in the browser and seven on the server, and the only check both of them do is the one they disagree about
items.summary: Notifio has exactly five form controls on its whole 38 page site. Four of them are the contact form on /help. I went to add a character counter to the message box, read both halves of the form properly first, and found that the two halves do not agree about what a valid submission is. ContactForm.tsx is 133 lines and all of its validation is HTML attributes: {/* name */} {/* email */} {/* subject */} {/* message */} Four checks: three required attributes and one type="email". The submit handler adds none of its own: async function handleSubmit(e: React.FormEvent) { e.preventDefault(); setStatus("sending"); const res = await fetch("/api/contact", { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify(fields), }); ... } preventDefault, then straight to fetch. No trimming, no length check, no second look at the email. That is a defensible choice: client validation is a courtesy and the server is the authority, so duplicating rules in two languages is how they drift apart. items.title: HSTS Missing From HTTPS Server: Why It's Still Flagged and How to Fix It
items.summary: Your scan report says "HSTS Missing From HTTPS Server (RFC 6797)", you add one header, you rescan, and the finding is still there. That second part is why most people end up searching for it. The header itself is one line. The finding keeps coming back because a scanner checks the response you didn't look at: a redirect, a different hostname, an error page or another port. I found two of those on this site while writing this, so the curl output below is real. Here's what the scanner actually checks, the fix for IIS, ASP.NET Core, Nginx, Apache, Next.js and Cloudflare, and how to make sure the next scan comes back clean. items.title: A Million v7 GUIDs and Half Were Still Out of Order
items.summary: I moved a table's primary key off random GUIDs a little while back. The reason is the usual one: a clustered index hates random inserts. Every new row wants a spot in the middle of the index instead of the end, pages split, the thing fragments, and your inserts get slower the bigger the table gets. Version 7 GUIDs are the tidy fix. They carry a millisecond timestamp in their leading bytes, so new keys sort roughly in creation order and land near the end where the index wants them. Before I trusted that in production I wanted to see the ordering with my own eyes. So I did the dumbest thing that would show it: generate a pile of keys and count how many came out in order. The answer made me feel a bit silly. A v7 GUID isn't random all the way down. The first 48 bits are a Unix millisecond timestamp, then a handful of version and variant bits, then the rest is random. Two keys created in different milliseconds sort by those timestamps. That's the whole trick, and it's why people reach for Guid.CreateVersion7() as a key: time-ordered values append instead of scattering. One thing to pin down first. items.title: Why red ink vanishes under a red sheet, and how I made an iPhone do it
items.summary: I work on Red Sheet at W Lab. Students in Japan write answers in red or orange pen, lay a sheet of red plastic over the page, and the answers disappear while the black questions stay. Slide the sheet down and you check yourself one line at a time. Red Sheet is an iPhone and iPad app that does this to a photo of your own notebook. This post is about the engine that finds the ink and hides it. Red plastic passes red light and blocks the rest. Through it, white paper looks red and red ink looks red, so the ink has nothing to stand out against. Black ink reflects no red either way, so it stays dark. Green highlighter is the opposite case: it reflects almost no red, so through the sheet it turns nearly black and blocks the word under it. The obvious way to copy that on a phone is to take the photo's red channel and tint it. I kept that version in the code as a comparison, and it fails on real photos. A phone photo of a notebook has a shadow across it, warm indoor light, greyish recycled paper. items.title: I Sorted Two Million Rows to Keep Ten
items.summary: A leaderboard endpoint I wrote returns the ten highest-scoring players, and for a while I never thought about it twice. Ten rows out, done. Then it started showing up in our gen0 collection graphs during traffic spikes, which made no sense to me, because the response is ten rows. The allocation counter disagreed, and that counter has never once flattered me. Here's the line that did it, more or less: var top = players .OrderByDescending(p => p.Score) .Take(10) .ToList(); It reads exactly like what I want. Sort by score, take ten. The problem is the order of operations under the hood. OrderByDescending doesn't know I only want ten until Take shows up later in the chain, so it buffers every player into an internal array first, then sorts enough of it to hand ten back. To return ten rows, it holds all of them at once. On a small table nobody notices. On two million rows it's a very different graph. I didn't want to argue from a hunch, so I wrote the smallest honest version I could. Two million rows of (id, score), built once up front so the data itself doesn't land on the scorecard. items.title: Writing Firmware in Swift: A Practical Look at Embedded Swift
items.summary: Most of us know Swift as the language behind iPhone, Mac, and server apps. But Swift can also go somewhere far smaller: microcontrollers. With Embedded Swift, you can compile Swift for tiny chips that have traditionally been programmed almost entirely in C and C++, and bring Swift's safety and clarity along with you. In this post I'll walk through what Embedded Swift actually is, what's different from everyday Swift, and what I'd want to know before picking up a dev board. Embedded Swift isn't a new language. It's a compiler mode, shown publicly at WWDC 2024, that generates small, standalone binaries that don't need the full Swift runtime. Think of it as a deliberately trimmed subset of Swift: it keeps everything that can be compiled into compact, predictable machine code, and drops the features that rely on a heavyweight runtime. That makes it possible to run Swift on chips with a few hundred KB of flash and only tens of KB of RAM (sometimes even less). items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a "general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode." By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. [...] Researcher Will Dormann said in an interview that he has been able to reproduce the exploit and that it works as described, but not on all versions of Windows 11. But there's a catch, he said. "The requirements are important in that it seems to require Windows 26H2, and one that has existed for more than 90 days, it seems," he explained. And whether logic the package adds to that step later still runs at all depends on whether the subclass remembered to call base. items.title: Stitching Photos into One Long Image in Swift: Common Width, a Height Cap, and One Photo in Memory at a Time
items.summary: A long image is the simplest way to post a set of photos as one thing: a trip, a recipe, a product from every angle. Stack the photos top to bottom, export one file, done. The first version most of us write is also simple: load every photo as a UIImage, add up the heights, draw them into a UIGraphicsImageRenderer, save. It works on the simulator with five screenshots. Then someone picks twelve 48-megapixel photos, two of them shot sideways, and the app either dies or produces a 9,000 × 60,000 pixel file that no social app will show at full size. I build BatchMark, an on-device photo app for iPhone, and its Photo Stories feature joins a set of finished photos into one long image. This post is a teaching extract of the problems you hit when you build that kind of stitcher, not the app's source. Everything here is ImageIO and Core Graphics, no third-party code. The approach has four parts: Read each photo's pixel size without decoding it. Plan the layout: one common width, heights scaled to match, total height capped. Eastern time that the nationwide flight traffic halt came "following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." items.title: Build Buddy, after the week: I tested my own fix on new samples
items.summary: Builders Week is over, but a reader's suggestion left one question open. Quick recap: Build Buddy asks a local Gemma 3 4B to fix C# compiler errors, then checks each fix by rebuilding and running the program. A fix only counts if it builds and prints the expected output. On my six samples, Gemma scored 5/6. The one failure was CS0161: the fix compiled, but added two extra Console.WriteLine calls. A reader suggested treating that as a known failure case and changing the prompt. One sentence, "Keep the program's behaviour and console output exactly the same," took it to 6/6. I wrote the rule after seeing the six samples fail, and I tested it on the same six. That's the classic way to fool yourself. A fix tuned on the test can pass the test without being any good. So I added four new samples the rule had never seen, each with one planted error and an expected.txt. I checked every answer key by running a hand-written correct fix first, because on Day 1 one of my own test cases was broken. Held-out sample Planted error Should print unassigned local CS0165: total used before it's set 12 max missing return CS0161: Max doesn't always return 7 int to bool CS0029: an int used as a bool True

items.title: Lego's BrickLink Marketplace Back Online After Week-Long Outage Caused By 'Cyber Incident'
items.summary: LEGO's BrickLink marketplace is back online after a week-long outage caused by what the company described as a "cyber incident," during which an unauthorized third party accessed some user data. Details about exactly what data was accessed remain unclear. The site went offline on November 5 and remained unavailable until November 12, preventing users from buying or selling LEGO sets and parts during the busy holiday shopping season. According to Brick Fanatics, LEGO initially described the outage as "necessary work" before confirming that the platform had suffered a security incident. In an email to users, LEGO acknowledged that "some of the information associated with your account was accessed and disclosed by an unauthorized party," including potentially usernames and IP addresses. However, the company insisted that "your password, postal address, and financial information were not disclosed." Those assurances have since come under scrutiny following reports of convincing phishing emails containing detailed personal and purchase information. items.title: Mozilla to Shut Down Solo, Deleting Users' Websites and Data
items.summary: Mozilla is shutting down Solo, its AI-powered website builder and hosting service, on November 30. A notice on the Soloist.ai homepage reads: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026." The Register reports: Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. Some 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them -- complete with custom domain names. Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ, users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images. The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com, with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: BriefBar: A native macOS menu bar & widget for GitHub PRs, Azure DevOps, and Copilot sessions
items.summary: Constantly jumping between browser tabs and terminal windows just to check if an Azure DevOps pipeline finished, a GitHub PR needs review, or a local GitHub Copilot session is waiting on input kills focus. I built brief-bar to put all of that into a single glanceable macOS menu bar popover and desktop widget. brief-bar is a native Swift/SwiftUI utility designed around opt-in developer data sources and strict local privacy: Unified Dev Status: Track GitHub PRs, Azure DevOps items/pipelines, and local GitHub Copilot sessions from one menu bar icon or macOS desktop widget. Every source is strictly opt-in—you only enable what you actually use. On-Device Apple Intelligence Summaries: Instead of dumping raw notification lists, brief-bar uses Apple's on-device Foundation Models to generate a quick brief of what needs your attention. Because it runs 100% locally via Apple Intelligence, there are no extra API keys to configure and your work metadata never leaves your Mac. Zero Electron Bloat: Built natively with SwiftUI and WidgetKit so it uses minimal memory and feels like a built-in part of macOS. You can install it directly via Homebrew or compile it from source: brew tap mnsn/brief-bar

items.title: Metering a Free Tier by Words Instead of Days in a Mac App
items.summary: On November 11, DraftKey shipped two releases about six hours apart. Version 0.1.61 made the app free to try with 2,000 words of writing help per Mac. Version 0.1.62 cut that to 500 words, added a warning when about 100 words are left, and changed what the app looks like once the allowance runs out. Both release notes are public, and they are the source for every DraftKey detail in this post. We build DraftKey, a Mac app for Tab autocomplete and rewrites you review before they are inserted. This is not a pricing post. It is about the engineering decisions hiding behind a sentence like "every Mac gets 500 free words," because almost none of them are obvious until you have to ship one. The default trial for desktop software is a clock: 7 or 14 days, then a paywall. A clock is easy to build and easy to explain. It is also a poor match for a tool you use in short bursts. Someone installs a writing helper on a Monday, uses it twice, gets busy, and comes back on day 15 to a locked app they never really tried. items.title: Volume zero is not mute
items.summary: With the volume at zero, my MacBook's speakers were still playing. Quietly enough that you only notice in a quiet room, but they were playing. On a Mac, volume and mute are two separate things. Volume is a number between 0 and 1. Mute is a switch. CoreAudio keeps them as two properties on the output device, and nothing forces them to agree. The number is a position on the device's range, and the device reports that range in decibels. So I asked the built-in speakers for theirs: var range = AudioValueRange() var size = UInt32(MemoryLayout .size) var a = AudioObjectPropertyAddress( mSelector: kAudioDevicePropertyVolumeRangeDecibels, mScope: kAudioDevicePropertyScopeOutput, mElement: kAudioObjectPropertyElementMain) AudioObjectGetPropertyData(device, &a, 0, nil, &size, &range) print(range.mMinimum, range.mMaximum) // -63.5 0.0 The bottom of the range is −63.5 dB. That is very quiet. It is not off. Usually nobody notices, because macOS flips the mute switch as well when the volume arrives at zero. items.title: Why a Mac Writing Helper Needs Two Permissions, and Why It Still Refuses Password Fields
items.summary: A writing helper that works inside someone else's text field has to ask macOS for a lot of trust. Accessibility permission is how an app reads and, if you approve it, replaces text in another app. Input Monitoring is how it can see keyboard events while you are in Mail, Notes, or a browser. Those are two different Privacy & Security toggles, and they should be. People are right to pause on both. We build DraftKey, a Mac app for Tab autocomplete and rewrites you review before they are inserted. This post is about the permission model behind a helper like that: why two system permissions are required, how we ask for them, and the cases we refuse even after you have said yes. The general mechanics come from Apple's public documentation, linked at the end. The product rules come from the shipped app's own wording, including the Apps & privacy section in Settings. Apple documents these as separate resources, and System Settings treats them that way. Accessibility is under Privacy & Security. The 21-year-old computer science major helped collect hundreds of signatures earlier this year from students, faculty, alumni and residents to demand that Stanford drop its current Flock contract and codify safeguards for similar tech tools the school may use in the future. The fear, Nguyen says, is that these cameras, which show where a vehicle was at a certain point in time, can be exploited to victimize vulnerable people. Stanford cut ties with Flock this summer, and it’s not alone. The privacy reckoning over the company’s surveillance cameras is gaining momentum at schools nationwide. items.title: FAA Expands AI Advice to Manage Air Traffic Congestion Across Entire US Airspace
items.summary: The FAA is expanding its $875 million AI-powered SMART system to all 22 U.S. air traffic control centers across the country. Since being implemented over Washington, DC, on September 21, the system has helped reroute 180 flights, saving an average of 10 minutes and nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight. Ars Technica reports: The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about "weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics" to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft. However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency. Furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system "cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft," the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. items.title: Euclid Mission Data Release Spans More Than 900 Million Galaxies
items.summary: The European Space Agency has released the largest dataset yet from its Euclid space telescope, containing 1.7 petabytes of observations covering more than 900 million galaxies. "The data unveiled on Thursday covered a survey of the sky equal to about 9,500 times the size of the moon as viewed from Earth," reports Reuters. "The mission's goal is to complete the "largest-ever three-dimensional atlas of the cosmos, spanning more than a third of the sky, in 2031." From the report: "It marks a major milestone for ESA's Euclid mission and for everyone involved," said astrophysicist Valeria Pettorino, ESA's Euclid project scientist. Euclid, launched from Florida in 2023, is gathering data on how the universe has expanded and how its structure has formed over time while amassing information about the nature of dark energy and dark matter and the role of gravity on large scales. "Euclid will not just take images of galaxies in the sky, in two dimensions, but will also measure their distance, the third dimension. items.title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?
items.summary: It is built of wood, resembles an Ikea and its power is totally renewable. Plus, it was built with the local community in mind. Is this facility in Falun the best datacentre in the world? ‘It was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden, which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms. One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. Huge panels of cross-laminated timber arrived at the site pre-cut, and were assembled by crane according to instructions, like flatpack furniture. Aesthetically, this section of the datacentre is more like an Ikea before the fit-out, a cavernous, echoey, immaculately clean hangar. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together. items.title: Handing over humanity (22 minute read)
items.summary: Some AI experts believe that once we achieve superintelligence, humans will be permanently disempowered, and we shall all be ruled by an AI god. This might not be such a desirable outcome, as humans have a natural desire for freedom. The arrangement will probably not work, as keeping power responsive to human needs has required checks developed over centuries, sustained by repeated feedback from the real world and correction, and there's no reason to keep that equilibrium stable once humans have surrendered all control. Humans have the ability now to steer the technology in a way that will not lead to a complete replacement of human judgment.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

items.title: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
items.summary: Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them. After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. Novel software is something that has fundamentally not existed before. Writing novel software with agents is challenging, as they are not trained on the task. Not a lot of software is novel, which is fine, as there is still a ton of value in the interpolative stuff.

items.summary: Linium is a two-person research lab that is trying to train its own generative video models entirely from scratch, aiming to create tools to democratize access to animation. items.title: Harness 2: executing agent code as it streams (6 minute read)
items.summary: Framer's Harness 2 significantly upgrades the agent's execution process, allowing entire workflows in one program, achieving up to 33% cost reduction and 20% faster execution. The redesign also replaces DSL with method calls for real-time updates, making task execution streamlined for both in-app and external agents, reducing tool steps by 43% and cached input tokens by 39% per message.

items.summary: Swarms are AI systems where multiple agents cooperate towards a shared goal. This post discusses a technique called collective inference-time scaling, where agents scale the amount of useful work performed in parallel and the communication needed to achieve it. It also explains how to design incentives for parallel work, and covers the general topic of designing incentives for reinforcement learning.

items.title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool (9 minute read)
items.summary: Agents are collapsing their entire tool catalog into one 'exec' tool. This allows models to write short scripts that chain, combine, and await actions inside isolated sandboxes. Models can now reliably combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass. In the previous standard tool-calling model, agents could only perform single actions, but the exec tool allows them to perform multiple actions.
